title: A Ten Is Ten Ones
keyIdea: Ten ones can be bundled into one group called a ten. A ten rod is 10 cubes stuck together, so 1 ten and 10 ones are the same amount. In a two-digit number the left digit counts tens and the right digit counts ones: 13 is 1 ten and 3 ones, and the 0 in 10 means no ones are left over. Swapping 10 ones for a ten never changes how many there are.

kid: Count out 10 cubes. Snap them into one tall stick. Now it is one ten. It is still 10 cubes. We just put them in a bundle.
Look at 13. The 1 is for one ten. The 3 is for three ones. So 13 is a ten stick and 3 loose cubes.
Got lots of loose ones? Count 10 of them and snap them into a stick. You swap 10 ones for 1 ten. You still have just as many cubes.
A ten stick is one thing, but it is worth 10. So 1 ten is more than 9 ones, even though 9 ones are more bits.
adult: This is the start of place value. US Common Core 1.NBT.B.2a says first graders should understand that 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones, called a ten, and 1.NBT.B.2b and 2c extend that to the teen numbers (a ten and some ones) and the decades (some tens and 0 ones). In England, the Year 1 and Year 2 programmes of study ask children to count in tens and to recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number.

The big step is unitising: seeing ten things as one unit while still knowing it is ten. Base-ten blocks (a rod of 10 and single unit cubes), bundles of straws and a tens-and-ones chart all show it. Exchanging, sometimes called regrouping, is swapping 10 ones for 1 ten or back again; the amount never changes, only how it is grouped. That idea later carries all of column addition and subtraction.

Common mistakes to watch for: counting a ten rod as 1, so 2 rods and 4 cubes becomes 6; writing the digits the wrong way round, so 1 ten and 7 ones becomes 71; thinking that more pieces means more, so 15 ones looks bigger than 2 tens; thinking that cubes vanish in a swap; and reading the 0 in 10 or 30 as nothing at all rather than as a zero that holds the ones place and says no extra ones.

In the lab your child bundles 10 loose cubes into a ten, reads three numbers built from rods and cubes, circles 10 ones to swap them for a ten and sees the total stay the same, builds 17, 30 and 10 on a tens-and-ones chart (10 ones swap themselves for a ten), and compares a ten with piles of ones.

familyTip: Bundle drinking straws or lolly sticks into tens with a hair band, and keep the rest loose. Grab a handful, bundle what you can, then say the number: 2 bundles and 6 loose is 26. Ask: did we lose any straws when we bundled them?

visual.caption: Is it worth exactly 10? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: bundle 10 ones into a ten, read tens and ones, swap 10 ones for a ten, build numbers on a chart and compare a ten with ones.

practice.prompt: How many ones are in 1 ten?
practice.hint: Picture a ten stick. Count the cubes in it one by one.
practice.explain: A ten is 10 ones stuck together, so 1 ten is the same as 10 ones.

practice.prompt: {t} tens and {o} ones. What number is that?
practice.hint: Count the tens in tens: 10, 20, 30 and so on. Then count on {o} ones.
practice.explain: {t} tens is {=t*10}. Count on {o} ones to get {=t*10+o}.

practice.prompt: You have {n} loose cubes. You snap 10 into a ten stick. How many loose cubes are left?
practice.hint: The ten stick uses 10 cubes. Take 10 away from {n}.
practice.explain: {n} is 1 ten and {=n-10} ones, so {=n-10} cubes are still loose.

practice.prompt: Which is more: 2 tens or 15 ones?
practice.hint: Turn the tens into ones. How many ones are in 2 tens?
practice.explain: 2 tens is 20 ones, and 20 is more than 15. More bits does not mean more.

pool.prompt: How many ones are the same as {t} tens?
pool.hint: Each ten is 10 ones. Count in tens {t} times.
pool.explain: {t} tens is {t} lots of 10, which is {=t*10} ones.

pool.prompt: What number is 1 ten and {o} ones?
pool.hint: Start at 10 for the ten. Count on {o} more.
pool.explain: 1 ten is 10. Count on {o} ones to get {=10+o}.

pool.prompt: Mia sees 2 ten sticks and 4 cubes. She says it is 6. What went wrong?
choices: She counted each ten stick as 1
pool.hint: How many cubes are in one ten stick?
pool.explain: Each stick is 10 cubes, so 2 sticks is 20. With 4 more it is 24, not 6.

pool.prompt: How do you write 1 ten and 7 ones?
pool.hint: The tens digit goes on the left, then the ones digit.
pool.explain: Tens go first, so 1 ten and 7 ones is written 17. 71 would be 7 tens and 1 one.

pool.prompt: You swap 10 loose ones for 1 ten. What happens to how many cubes you have?
pool.hint: Did any cubes go in the bin, or did they just get snapped together?
pool.explain: Swapping only groups the cubes. 10 ones and 1 ten are the same amount, so the total stays the same.

pool.prompt: What does the 0 in 30 tell you?
choices: There are no ones left over
pool.hint: Which place is the 0 in: the tens or the ones?
pool.explain: 30 is 3 tens and 0 ones. The 0 holds the ones place and says there are no extra ones.

pool.hint: The left digit counts the tens.
pool.explain: 46 is 4 tens and 6 ones, so there are 4 tens. 46 is the whole number.

pool.hint: Add up the ones in each card. Which makes 10?
pool.explain: 5 ones and 5 ones is 10 ones, which is 1 ten. 9 ones is one short and 1 ten and 1 one is 11.
